meta.tagline: The city of literature, pub talk and rainbow-colored doors

overview.title: Welcome to Dublin
overview.intro: Dublin impresses not with size but with sound: the fiddle spilling out of a pub, the busker's guitar, and the Irish appetite for storytelling that never runs dry. Joyce, Wilde, Beckett and four Nobel laureates walked these streets; the thousand-year-old Book of Kells glows in Trinity's library, and Georgian doors line up like a rainbow. The Liffey splits the city in two, but pub culture unites everyone: here a stranger is simply 'a friend we haven't met yet'. Bring your umbrella and your sense of humor — Dublin will make use of both.

local_word.definition: Ireland's untranslatable word: conversation, fun, the joy of good company — all at once. 'What's the craic?' means both 'how are you' and 'what's happening'; if someone says 'the craic was mighty', the night was legendary. Craic can't be bought — it arrives on its own once you join the conversation in a pub.

rules.title: Enter the pub for the talk, not the drink
rules.description: A Dublin pub is not a bar but a living room: lean on the counter, say 'What's the craic?', and the rest follows on its own. If there's live trad music, talk between songs and listen while they play — respect for the musicians is the first article of pub etiquette.

rules.title: Give your Guinness its two minutes
rules.description: A proper Guinness is poured in two stages: the barman rests the glass at three-quarters, then tops it up. Don't reach for it during the wait — let the surge settle and the barman finish the job. Take the first sip through the cream; in Dublin this is a ritual, and hurrying it is bad form.

rules.title: Book Kells and Kilmainham ahead
rules.description: Tickets for the Book of Kells and Kilmainham Gaol sell out days in advance: buy both online and plan around your timed slots. Turning up at the door only to hit the 'sold out' sign is Dublin's most classic tourist heartbreak.

tip.label: The Dublin philosophy
tip.text: The weather plays all four seasons in a day here and nobody minds: when rain hits, step into a pub; when the sun breaks, head for a park. Dublin loves those who keep plans loose — the best moments were never on the schedule anyway.

transport.title: Getting Around
transport.intro: The center is walkable; the Luas tram and the DART coastal train weave the city, green buses reach everywhere — the keyword is Leap Card.

items.title: Arriving from the airport
items.description: There's no train from Dublin Airport to the center: the Dublin Express and Aircoach buses do it in 30–40 minutes, with night services too. Buy your ticket online — a taxi costs three times the same road.

items.title: The Luas tram
items.description: Two lines, green and red, cross the city: Trinity, St Stephen's Green and Jervis are the key stops. Ride with a Leap Card — always cheaper than single tickets, and it works on buses too.

items.title: The DART coastal train
items.description: The train strings the coastline from Howth to Bray along the bay: window seat, Irish Sea views. A pleasant half-hour ride for the Howth escape — go early on weekends.

items.title: A walkable center
items.description: Trinity, Temple Bar, Grafton Street and St Stephen's Green are steps apart: the center can be walked in half a day. For rain breaks, the network of pubs and bookshops stands ready on every corner.

items.title: Dublin Bikes
items.description: City bike stations spread across the center: practical and cheap for short hops. The canal-side routes — the Grand Canal way — are the loveliest pedaling line; keep to quiet streets until left-hand traffic feels natural.

callout.label: Card tip
callout.text: The Leap Visitor Card gives 1, 3 or 7 days of unlimited transport and covers the airport bus: for stays beyond two days it almost always pays off. Automatic fare capping keeps your daily spend at the ceiling — the card does the ticket math for you.

stay.title: Where to Stay
stay.intro: In Dublin choosing a neighborhood means choosing your night soundtrack: Temple Bar's hubbub, Georgian elegance, or canal-side calm.

local_word.definition: Dublin slang for 'home': a 'free gaff' means nobody's home, 'come to my gaff' is an invitation. The word sums up the city's warmth — a Dubliner shares their home and their city quickly. Don't be surprised if you start calling your own lodgings 'my gaff' within two days.

items.name: Around Temple Bar
items.description: Inside the cobblestoned pub quarter: everything at your doorstep, and the night noise too. Practical for short stays built on walking — light sleepers should pick a street or two out.

items.name: St Stephen's Green & the Georgian quarter
items.description: The neighborhood of colorful-doored Georgian terraces and parks: Grafton Street shopping and the museums within walking distance. For waking up on Dublin's postcard side.

items.name: Smithfield & Stoneybatter
items.description: The northside's regenerating villages: third-wave coffee shops, craft-beer pubs, the Jameson distillery. One step off the tourist trail, prices one notch kinder.

items.name: Portobello
items.description: The villagey neighborhood along the Grand Canal: brunch cafes, quiet streets, a fifteen-minute walk to the center. For starting the day with a swan-lined canal stroll.

items.name: Ballsbridge
items.description: The southern district of embassies and tree-lined avenues: hotels with big rooms, quiet nights. A few stops to the center by DART or bus — the balanced pick for comfort-first travelers.

best_time.title: When to Go
best_time.intro: Dublin's weather surprises in every season and the city stays open in all of them: summer brings long days, March brings green, December brings lights.

items.label: Spring
items.name: Paddy's Day Spring
items.subtitle: Spring · St Patrick's festival, stretching days
items.description: On March 17th the city paints itself green: the St Patrick's Day parade is Dublin's biggest celebration. April and May bring blossoming parks and lengthening days, with crowds still below summer levels — the sweet season for city walking.

callout.label: March note
callout.text: In St Patrick's week hotels sell out months ahead and prices multiply: book early if you want the parade, skip the week if you don't. On parade day the pubs fill by noon — eat a solid breakfast.

items.label: Summer
items.name: Long Light Days
items.subtitle: Summer · Daylight until 22:00, festival calendar
items.description: Summer Dublin is generous: daylight lasts until ten, the parks fill with picnickers, and the Howth walks meet their golden hour. Bloomsday (June 16th) pours Joyce lovers onto the streets. Temperatures rarely pass 25°C — summer here is a cool gift.

callout.label: June tip
callout.text: On June 16th, Bloomsday, the city lives its Ulysses day: readings in period dress, lemon soap at Sweny's pharmacy, walks along the Joyce route. Catch the city of literature on its most literary day.

items.label: Autumn
items.name: Golden Parks
items.subtitle: Autumn · Orange St Stephen's Green, theatre season
items.description: The parks turn orange, the theatre festival fills the stages, and the pub fireplaces are lit: Dublin's most photogenic and most 'itself' season. Crowds thin and prices soften — the city returns to its locals and to those in the know.

callout.label: October tip
callout.text: In October the Dublin Theatre Festival is toured stage by stage: buy a ticket, then join the craic in a fireside pub afterwards. The Howth cliff walk is also at its year's best in autumn light — bring a windbreaker.

items.label: Winter
items.name: Firesides and Lights
items.subtitle: Winter · Early dark, warm pub evenings
items.description: The winter day is short and the pub is long: the Grafton Street lights come on, and trad sessions deepen in fireside rooms. Rain and wind are constant companions but snow is rare — a Dublin winter is the art of shivering outside and warming up inside.

callout.label: December tip
callout.text: In December choirs sing under the Grafton Street lights: escape the shopping crowds in the late afternoon and walk the lights calmly after 21:00. Instead of mulled wine, the Irish way: a hot whiskey by the fire.

eat.title: What to Eat
eat.intro: Irish cooking is the power of simplicity: good butter, fresh seafood, hearty stews — and beside them all, a properly poured pint.

local_word.definition: In Dublin, 'pint' means one thing: Guinness. The 568-milliliter glass is poured in a two-stage ritual and never hurried. 'A pint of plain is your only man,' wrote the city's poet — 'plain' being Guinness's old neighborhood name.

items.name: A properly poured Guinness
items.description: The barman rests the glass at three-quarters, the surge settles, the head is crowned: two minutes of patience, a velvet-textured reward. Take the first sip through the cream — in the city of St James's Gate this is not a drink but an identity.

items.name: Irish stew and Dublin coddle
items.description: Irish stew of lamb and potato is the classic; coddle, with sausages and onions, is Dublin's home secret. Both warm like a pub fireplace — the undisputed answer to a rainy noon.

items.name: Fish and chips
items.description: The newspaper-wrap days are gone but the tradition stands: crisp-battered cod, thick-cut chips, vinegar and salt. Buy from a century-old 'chipper' and eat by the canal — mind the seagulls.

items.name: Seafood chowder and brown bread
items.description: Creamy seafood chowder with Ireland's soda brown bread and salted butter: the signature duo of the coastal pubs. Have it on the Howth pier with the sea in view — the chowder thickens differently out there.

items.name: Boxty and the full Irish
items.description: Boxty, the potato pancake, is traditional cooking's hidden star; the full Irish — sausage, bacon, eggs, black and white pudding, beans — is a challenge to the day. Both hold you until noon — plan accordingly.
items.tag: A challenge to the day · full till noon

items.name: Irish coffee
items.description: Hot coffee, whiskey, brown sugar and a float of cream: invented by an Irish barman in the 1940s. Don't stir the cream — drink the coffee through it. The most elegant way to warm up on a cold day.
items.tag: Don't stir the cream · cold-day classic

callout.label: Table rule
callout.text: Pub food in Dublin isn't cheap, but it is filling: lunch specials run at half the evening price — put the big meal at noon and build the evening on soup and a pint. Don't dine in Temple Bar; two streets over, the same plate comes a third cheaper.

hidden_gems.title: Hidden Corners
hidden_gems.intro: Everyone sees Trinity and Temple Bar; these six are Dublin's book-scented, tucked-away corners.

items.name: Marsh's Library
items.description: Ireland's first public library, almost unchanged since 1707: oak shelves, reading cages and Swift's marginalia. In the cathedral's shadow, a sanctuary of silence the tourist flood walks straight past.

items.name: Iveagh Gardens
items.description: A Victorian garden hidden one street behind St Stephen's Green: fountains, a rose garden and a miniature maze. Eat your lunch sandwich in this walled oasis where locals escape — most tourists never learn it exists.

items.name: The Howth cliff walk
items.description: Half an hour by DART to the fishing village of Howth: a walk above the cliffs on the lighthouse loop, chowder on the pier afterwards. Seals see you off in the harbor — Dublin's sweetest half day.

items.name: Kilmainham Gaol
items.description: The prison where the leaders of the 1916 Rising spent their last days: cells, the yard and a striking guided tour. Ireland's independence story takes physical form in these corridors — book days ahead.

items.name: Sweny's Pharmacy
items.description: The chemist's shop Joyce immortalized in Ulysses, kept alive by volunteers: lemon soap is still sold, lunchtime readings still held. A tiny shop, an enormous literature — don't hesitate at the door; it's welcoming inside.

items.name: The Grand Canal and Kavanagh's bench
items.description: Patrick Kavanagh's statue sits on his bench by the canal: perch beside him, watch the swans, and remember him 'where there is water', just as the poet asked. The canal walk toward Portobello is Dublin's calmest route.

callout.label: Corner strategy
callout.text: Dublin's pearls hide one street behind the great landmarks: Marsh's behind the cathedral, Iveagh behind the Green, Sweny's across from Trinity. See the big stop, then turn immediately behind it — the city's true face sits in the alcoves.

traps.title: Tourist Traps
traps.intro: Dublin is a friendly city, but falling for the tourist bait is expensive; know these four and save your budget for the pints.

items.name: The Temple Bar price list
items.description: In the district's famous pubs a pint costs nearly double the city average; the live music is often a playlist tuned for tourists.
items.instead: Tour Temple Bar by day and take your photos; drink your pint and hear your trad session in a neighborhood pub: ask for places like The Cobblestone, where musicians play for themselves. The difference shows in the bill and in the craic.

items.name: Arriving ticketless at Kells and Kilmainham
items.description: Both icons run timed, capacity-limited entries: the sight greeting walk-ups most days is the 'sold out' sign.
items.instead: Book both online days ahead; for Kells the first morning slot is best for calm and for light. Check the Long Room's restoration status on the site too.

items.name: Green-hat-and-shamrock souvenir shops
items.description: Mass-produced 'Guaranteed Irish' sweaters and figurines sell at hand-knit Aran prices; for many, the only Irish thing is the label.
items.instead: Buy a real Aran sweater by reading the wool label and feeling the knit; for gifts choose Irish design shops and bookshops — a Dublin-printed book of poems outlives a shamrock figurine.

items.name: The airport taxi reflex
items.description: The center-to-airport taxi is both expensive and slow at rush hour: the meter runs as the Dublin Express passes you in the bus lane.
items.instead: Book the Dublin Express or Aircoach online: frequent departures, luggage space, fixed price. Night services cover early flights — consider a taxi only with a group and heavy bags.

callout.label: Golden rule
callout.text: Dublin money matters in one line: tickets for the icons in advance, pints from the neighborhood, gifts from the maker. The rest — parks, doors, cliffs, street music — is already free; the city's best face never asks for your wallet.

itinerary.title: Ready-Made Itineraries
itinerary.intro: If you hate planning, follow these flows. Times are flexible; keep the spirit, break the order.

plans.title: If You Have 1 Day
plans.subtitle: From the Book of Kells to a trad session

steps.title: Full Irish breakfast
steps.description: Start the day with a challenge: sausage, bacon, eggs, pudding. Full until noon — the plan is built on it.

steps.title: Trinity and the Book of Kells
steps.description: Stand before the thousand-year-old manuscript with your timed ticket, then walk the book cathedral of the Long Room. The morning slot is the calmest.

steps.title: Grafton Street and the Georgian doors
steps.description: Walk to the buskers' soundtrack, stretch to St Stephen's Green; make the photo tour of the rainbow doors around Merrion Square.

steps.title: Kilmainham Gaol
steps.description: The guided tour with your pre-booked ticket: Ireland's independence story in the cell corridors. A riverside walk on the way back.

steps.title: Chowder and the first pint
steps.description: Seafood chowder and brown bread in a fireside pub; beside it, a Guinness poured in two stages. Wait for the surge to settle — that's the ritual.

steps.title: Trad session night
steps.description: Fiddle, flute and bodhrán in a neighborhood pub: lean on the bar, say 'What's the craic?'. Talk between songs, silence while they play — the night stretches on its own.

plans.title: If You Have 3 Days
plans.subtitle: Literature, memory and cliffs — the full Dublin

steps.title: Classic Dublin
steps.description: The 1-day flow above: full Irish, Trinity and Kells, the Georgian doors, Kilmainham, chowder, a trad session.

steps.title: Alcoves and tastes
steps.description: Morning at Marsh's Library and the cathedral quarter; a walled-garden break in Iveagh Gardens at noon; afternoon at the Guinness Storehouse's Gravity Bar view or a distillery tour in Smithfield; evening of local food and craft pubs in Stoneybatter.

steps.title: Howth and farewell
steps.description: Morning DART to Howth: the cliff walk, the lighthouse loop, seals in the harbor; fish and chips or chowder on the pier at noon; lemon soap at Sweny's and a canal pause on Kavanagh's bench on the way back; farewell night with an Irish coffee by a pub fire.

phrases.title: 5-Word Survival Kit
phrases.intro: Dublin English comes with its own dictionary; these five phrases make you half a local in the pub and on the street.

items.meaning: How's it going, what's happening? — the official opening of pub conversation
Cheers! — Irish for 'health'; eye contact required as the pints rise
Fine, okay, no problem — the Dubliner's answer to everything: 'It's grand!'
Well done, good on you — approval, Dublin style
Thanks / goodbye / cheers — the multi-purpose word you'll hear fifty times a day

checklist.completion_message: Fair play! You've lived the city of literature and craic the way it deserves!
